title: Escaping The Shadow Of Bell’s Theorem In Network Nonlocality
authors: Maria Ciudad Alañón, Emanuel-Cristian Boghiu, Paolo Abiuso, And Elie Wolfe
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2213 (2026).

The possibility of nonclassicality in networks unrelated to Bell’s original eponymous theorem has recently attracted significant interest. Here, we identify a sufficient condition for being “outside the shadow of Bell’s theorem” and introduce a testable criterion capable of certifying the novelty of instances of network-nonclassicality which we call minimal network nonclassicality. We provide examples of minimally network nonclassical correlations realizable in quantum theory as well as examples coming from more exotic operational probabilistic theories. In particular, we apply these concepts to the simplest configuration of the 3-chain scenario (a.k.a. the bilocality scenario) to prove that certain correlations have escaped the shadow of Bell's theorem. While some of the examples herein are unprecedented, we also revisit more familiar examples of network nonclassicality in order to highlight the contrast between our approach versus prior approaches with respect to assessing novelty.

.
tldr: The paper introduces minimal network nonclassicality and a sufficient condition for correlations to escape the shadow of Bell's theorem, with examples in quantum theory and beyond.
motivation: Network nonlocality has attracted significant interest, but it is often unclear whether observed nonclassicality is genuinely novel or merely reducible to standard Bell nonlocality.
method: The authors define a testable criterion for being outside the shadow of Bell's theorem, called minimal network nonclassicality, and apply it to the 3-chain/bilocality scenario.
result: They provide examples of minimally network nonclassical correlations in quantum theory and exotic operational probabilistic theories, proving certain correlations escape Bell's shadow.
conclusion: This approach offers a sharper way to assess the novelty of network-nonclassicality and distinguishes it from prior approaches.

title: Quantifying Mixed-state Entanglement Via Partial Transpose And Realignment Moments
authors: Poetri Sonya Tarabunga And Tobias Haug
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2194 (2026).

Entanglement plays a crucial role in quantum information science and many-body physics, yet quantifying it in mixed quantum many-body systems has remained a notoriously difficult problem. Here, we introduce families of quantitative entanglement witnesses, constructed from partial transpose and realignment moments, which provide rigorous bounds on entanglement monotones as well as entanglement dimensionality. Our witnesses can be efficiently measured using SWAP tests or variants of Bell measurements, thus making them directly implementable on current hardware. Leveraging our witnesses, we present several novel results on entanglement properties of mixed states, both in quantum information and many-body physics. We develop efficient algorithms to test whether mixed states with bounded entropy have low or high entanglement, which previously was only possible for pure states. We also provide an efficient algorithm to test the Schmidt rank using only two-copy measurements, and the operator Schmidt rank using four-copy measurements. Further, our witnesses robustly certify the quantum circuit depth in the presence of noise, as well as the Schmidt rank of mixed states. Finally, we show that the entanglement phase diagram of Haar random states, quantified by the partial transpose negativity, can be fully established solely by computing our witness, a result that also applies to any state [MATH]-design. Our witnesses can also be efficiently computed for matrix product states, thus enabling the characterization of entanglement in extensive many-body systems. Finally, we make progress on the entanglement required for quantum cryptography, establishing rigorous limits on pseudoentanglement and pseudorandom density matrices with bounded entropy. Our work opens new avenues for quantifying entanglement in large and noisy quantum systems.

.
tldr: The paper introduces quantitative entanglement witnesses based on partial transpose and realignment moments for mixed quantum many-body states, with efficient measurement schemes and applications to entanglement detection, Schmidt rank certification, circuit depth, and pseudoentanglement.
motivation: Quantifying entanglement in mixed quantum many-body systems is notoriously difficult, and existing tools are largely limited to pure states or require impractical resources.
method: The authors construct families of entanglement witnesses from partial transpose and realignment moments, which yield rigorous bounds on entanglement monotones and dimensionality and can be measured via SWAP tests or Bell measurement variants.
result: They obtain efficient algorithms to test low/high entanglement for bounded-entropy mixed states, certify Schmidt rank with two-copy measurements and operator Schmidt rank with four-copy measurements, robustly certify quantum circuit depth under noise, and determine the entanglement phase diagram of Haar random states via partial transpose negativity.
conclusion: These witnesses enable practical quantification of entanglement in large noisy quantum systems and establish rigorous limits on pseudoentanglement and pseudorandom density matrices, opening new avenues for mixed-state entanglement characterization.

title: Non-stabilizerness And Violations Of Chsh Inequalities
authors: Stefano Cusumano, Lorenzo Campos Venuti, Simone Cepollaro, Immacolata de Simone, Gianluca Esposito, Daniele Iannotti, Barbara Jasser, Jovan Odavić, Michele Viscardi, And Alioscia Hamma
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2214 (2026).

We study quantitatively the interplay between entanglement and non-stabilizer resources in violating the CHSH inequalities. We show that, while non-stabilizer resources are necessary, they must have a specific structure, namely they need to be both asymmetric and (surprisingly) [MATH]. We employ stabilizer entropy (SE) to quantify the non-stabilizer resources involved and the probability of violation given the resources. We show how spectral quantities related to the flatness of entanglement spectrum and its relationship with non-local SE affect the CHSH inequality. Finally, we utilize these results – together with tools from representation theory – to construct a systematic way of building ensembles of states with higher probability of violation.

.
tldr: The paper quantitatively studies how non-stabilizer resources, quantified by stabilizer entropy, must be structured to enable violations of CHSH inequalities in entangled quantum states.
motivation: Entanglement alone is insufficient for certain Bell violations, and understanding the role of non-stabilizerness (magic) as a resource is crucial for quantum information tasks.
method: The authors use stabilizer entropy to measure non-stabilizer resources, analyze the entanglement spectrum's flatness, and employ representation theory to construct ensembles of states with higher CHSH violation probability.
result: They find that non-stabilizer resources must be both asymmetric and have a specific form to enable CHSH violations, and that spectral properties of the entanglement spectrum affect the violation probability.
conclusion: This work clarifies the interplay between entanglement and non-stabilizerness in Bell nonlocality and provides a systematic method for constructing states with enhanced violation probability.

title: Universal Purification Dynamics In Real Non-unitary Quantum Processes
authors: Federico Gerbino, Donghoon Kim, Guido Giachetti, Andrea de Luca And Xhek Turkeshi
abstract: We study purification dynamics in monitored quantum processes governed by ensembles of quantum circuits in different random-matrix symmetry classes. We analyze the universal aspects that emerge away from the measurement-induced phase transition and inside the volume/weak measurement phase and in the scaling limit of large time and Hilbert space dimension. We present two toy models that reveal two complementary visions and provide quantitative access to universal scaling: (i) a discrete-time dynamic in which each time step corresponds to multiplication by a Gaussian random matrix; (ii) weak continuous-time monitoring that induces a Dyson Brownian motion of the eigenvalues of the density matrix. The first approach provides an algebraic characterization based on rotational invariance emerging in Kraus’s operator space, focusing in particular on the unitary and orthogonal cases, respectively and , with the Dyson random-matrix index. The second approach, on the other hand, allows for a unified treatment for any , thanks to the mapping of the Fokker–Planck evolution of eigenvalues onto the Calogero–Sutherland integrable Hamiltonian diagonalized in terms of Jack polynomials. We provide explicit expressions for the universal decrease of Rényi entropies. We show that, approaching the universal scaling limit, numerical simulations of different models agree with each other and with our theoretical predictions. Our results clarify the existence of different classes of universality for the purification process in hybrid quantum systems, accessible in random circuit architectures and weak measurement protocols.
tldr: The paper studies universal purification dynamics in monitored quantum circuits using random matrix ensembles, deriving scaling laws for Rényi entropies via Dyson Brownian motion and Calogero-Sutherland integrability.
motivation: Understanding universal aspects of purification and entanglement dynamics in monitored quantum systems away from measurement-induced phase transitions and in the volume/weak measurement phase.
method: Two toy models: (i) discrete-time evolution by Gaussian random matrices with rotational invariance in Kraus operator space; (ii) continuous weak monitoring mapped to Dyson Brownian motion and Fokker-Planck evolution diagonalized by Jack polynomials.
result: Explicit expressions for the universal decrease of Rényi entropies are obtained, and numerical simulations of different models agree with theoretical predictions in the universal scaling limit.
conclusion: The results clarify distinct universality classes for purification in hybrid quantum systems, accessible in random circuit architectures and weak measurement protocols.

title: Information Gain And Measurement Disturbance For Quantum Agents
authors: Arthur O T Pang, Noah Lupu-Gladstein, Y Batuhan Yilmaz, C Pria Dobney, Rui Jie Tang, Aharon Brodutch And Aephraim M Steinberg
abstract: The traditional formalism of quantum measurement (hereafter ‘TQM’) describes processes where some properties of quantum states are extracted and stored as classical information. While TQM is a natural and appropriate description of how humans interact with quantum systems, it is silent on the question of how a more general, quantum, agent would do so. How do we describe the observation of a system by an agent with the ability to store not only classical information but quantum states in its memory? In this paper, we extend the idea of measurement to a more general class of sensors for quantum agents which interact with a system in such a way that the agent’s memory stores information (classical or quantum) about the system under study. For appropriate sensory interactions, the quantum agent may ‘learn’ more about the system than would be possible under any set of classical measurements—but as we show, this comes at the cost of additional measurement disturbance. We experimentally demonstrate such a system and characterize the tradeoffs by considering the channel capacity required to erase the effect of a measurement.
tldr: Extends quantum measurement theory to quantum agents that store quantum information, showing they can learn more about a system than classical agents but at the cost of additional disturbance.
motivation: Traditional quantum measurement only describes how classical information is extracted, leaving open how a quantum agent with quantum memory would observe a system.
method: Develops a general framework for sensory interactions of quantum agents with a system and experimentally demonstrates the resulting information-disturbance tradeoffs by analyzing the channel capacity required to erase measurement effects.
result: For suitable interactions, a quantum agent may gain more information than possible under any set of classical measurements, but this comes with additional measurement disturbance; the tradeoff is characterized via erasure channel capacity.
conclusion: The work generalizes measurement theory to quantum agents and reveals fundamental limits on information gain and disturbance, supported by experimental demonstration.

title: Spatial Structure Of Multipartite Entanglement At Measurement Induced Phase Transitions
authors: James Allen And William Witczak-Krempa
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2211 (2026).

We study multiparty entanglement near measurement induced phase transitions (MIPTs), which arise in ensembles of local quantum circuits built with unitaries and measurements. In contrast to equilibrium quantum critical transitions, where entanglement is short-ranged, MIPTs possess long-range k-party genuine multiparty entanglement (GME) characterized by an infinite hierarchy of entanglement exponents for k[MATH]2. First, we represent the average spread of entanglement with "entanglement clusters", and use them to conjecture general exponent relations: 1) classical dominance, 2) monotonicity, 3) subadditivity. We then introduce measure-weighted graphs to construct such clusters in general circuits. Second, we obtain the exact entanglement exponents for a 1d MIPT in a measurement-only circuit that maps to percolation by exploiting non-unitary conformal field theory. The exponents, which we numerically verify, obey the inequalities. We also extend the construction to a 2d MIPT that maps to classical 3d percolation, and numerically find the first entanglement exponents. Our results provide a firm ground to understand the multiparty entanglement of MIPTs, and more general ensembles of quantum circuits.

.
tldr: This paper characterizes the spatial structure of multipartite entanglement near measurement-induced phase transitions, introducing entanglement clusters and deriving exact entanglement exponents for 1D and 2D models.
motivation: MIPTs exhibit long-range multipartite entanglement unlike equilibrium critical points, but the spatial organization and exponent hierarchy are not well understood.
method: They define entanglement clusters and measure-weighted graphs to conjecture exponent relations (classical dominance, monotonicity, subadditivity), and compute exact exponents for a 1D measurement-only circuit mapping to percolation via non-unitary CFT, with numerical verification and extension to 2D.
result: The exact exponents satisfy the conjectured inequalities, and the 2D numerical results provide the first entanglement exponents, confirming the framework.
conclusion: The work establishes a foundation for understanding multiparty entanglement in MIPTs and general quantum circuit ensembles.

title: Floquetifying Stabiliser Codes With Distance-preserving Rewrites
authors: Benjamin Rodatz, Boldizsár Poór, And Aleks Kissinger
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2202 (2026).

Stabiliser codes with large weight measurements can be challenging to implement fault-tolerantly. To overcome this, we propose a Floquetification procedure which, given a stabiliser code, synthesises a novel Floquet code that only uses single- and two-qubit operations. Moreover, this procedure preserves the distance and number of logicals of the original code. The new Floquet code requires additional physical qubits. This overhead is linear in the weight of the largest measurement of the original code. Our method is based on the ZX calculus, a graphical language for representing and rewriting quantum circuits. However, a problem arises with the use of ZX in the context of rewriting error-correcting codes: ZX rewrites generally do not preserve code distance. Tackling this issue, we define the notion of distance-preserving rewrite that enables the transformation of error-correcting codes without changing their distance. These distance-preserving rewrites are used to decompose arbitrary weight stabiliser measurements into quantum circuits with single- and two-qubit operations. As we only use distance-preserving rewrites, we are guaranteed that a single error in the resulting circuit creates at most a single error on the data qubits. These decompositions enable us to generalise the Floquetification procedure of Townsend-Teague et al [83] to arbitrary stabiliser codes, provably preserving the distance and number of logicals of the original code.

.
tldr: The paper introduces a Floquetification procedure using distance-preserving ZX-calculus rewrites to transform arbitrary stabiliser codes into Floquet codes that use only single- and two-qubit operations while preserving code distance and logical count.
motivation: Stabiliser codes with high-weight measurements are challenging to implement fault-tolerantly, and existing Floquetification methods are limited to specific codes.
method: They define distance-preserving rewrites in the ZX calculus to decompose arbitrary weight stabiliser measurements into circuits with single- and two-qubit operations, then use these rewrites to synthesise a novel Floquet code.
result: The resulting Floquet code preserves the distance and number of logicals of the original stabiliser code, requires overhead linear in the largest measurement weight, and guarantees that a single circuit error causes at most one data-qubit error.
conclusion: This generalises the Floquetification procedure to arbitrary stabiliser codes, providing a fault-tolerant route for high-weight codes.

title: Hierarchical Separation Of Relaxation Timescales From Spectral Localization Bounds
authors: Alex Stewart-Bozzo, Jakub Garwoła, Brett Min And Dvira Segal
abstract: We investigate the dissipative dynamics of multilevel quantum systems strongly coupled either to a lossy cavity mode or directly to a bosonic environment. By deriving spectral localization bounds, we establish conditions under which strong system-bath coupling gives rise to a hierarchy of population relaxation timescales. Our approach builds on the reaction-coordinate polaron-transform framework. By mapping the original strong-coupling problem onto an effective weakly dissipative model, we analyze the spectrum of the resulting Liouvillian superoperator through localization bounds. For the generalized V model, we find that strong system-bath coupling gives rise to a bright–dark structure in the effective system-bath coupling operator: a single collective mode remains strongly coupled to the environment, while the remaining modes become progressively dark. Consequently, the dynamics separate into fast and slow sectors and, at finite coupling strengths, develop a hierarchy of population relaxation timescales. Numerical simulations based on both secular and non-secular quantum master equations corroborate the emergence of timescale separation and the pronounced slowing down of dissipative dynamics at strong coupling. Our results reveal a general mechanism underlying anomalously slow relaxation in strongly coupled open quantum systems and provide a route for engineering long-lived states through system-environment interactions.
tldr: The paper derives spectral localization bounds to show that strong system-bath coupling can generate a hierarchy of population relaxation timescales in multilevel open quantum systems.
motivation: Strongly coupled open quantum systems often exhibit anomalously slow relaxation, but a general mechanism and rigorous bounds for the emergence of relaxation timescale hierarchies are lacking.
method: The authors use the reaction-coordinate polaron-transform framework to map the strong-coupling problem onto an effective weakly dissipative model and analyze the resulting Liouvillian spectrum through spectral localization bounds, corroborating with secular and non-secular master equation simulations.
result: For the generalized V model, strong system-bath coupling produces a bright–dark structure in the effective coupling operator, with one collective bright mode and progressively dark modes, leading to separated fast and slow dynamical sectors and a hierarchy of population relaxation timescales.
conclusion: The work reveals a general mechanism for slow relaxation in strongly coupled open quantum systems and suggests a route to engineer long-lived states via system-environment interactions.

title: Gibbs State Preparation For Commuting Hamiltonian: Mapping To Classical Gibbs Sampling
authors: Yeongwoo Hwang And Jiaqing Jiang
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2209 (2026).

Gibbs state preparation, or Gibbs sampling, is a key computational technique extensively used in physics, statistics, and other scientific fields. Recent efforts for designing fast mixing Gibbs samplers for quantum Hamiltonians have largely focused on commuting local Hamiltonians (CLHs), a non-trivial subclass of Hamiltonians which include highly entangled systems such as the Toric code and quantum double model. Most previous Gibbs samplers relied on simulating the Davies generator, which is a Lindbladian associated with the thermalization process in nature. Instead of using the Davies generator, we design a different Gibbs sampler for various CLHs by giving a reduction to classical Hamiltonians, in the sense that one can efficiently prepare the Gibbs state for some CLH [MATH] on a quantum computer as long as one can efficiently do classical Gibbs sampling for the corresponding classical Hamiltonian [MATH]. We demonstrate that our Gibbs sampler is able to replicate state-of-the-art results as well as prepare the Gibbs state in regimes which were previously unknown, such as the low temperature region, as long as there exists fast mixing Gibbs samplers for the corresponding classical Hamiltonians. Our reductions are as follows. – If [MATH] is a 2-local qudit CLH, then [MATH] is a 2-local qudit classical Hamiltonian. – If [MATH] is a 4-local qubit CLH on 2D lattice and there are no classical qubits, then [MATH] is a 2-local qudit classical Hamiltonian on a planar graph. As an example, our algorithm can prepare the Gibbs state for the (defected) Toric code at any non-zero temperature in [MATH] time. – If [MATH] is a 4-local qubit CLH on 2D lattice and there are classical qubits, assuming that quantum terms are uniformly correctable, then [MATH] is a constant-local classical Hamiltonian.

.
tldr: The paper designs a quantum Gibbs sampler for commuting local Hamiltonians via a reduction to classical Gibbs sampling, enabling efficient preparation of thermal states including low-temperature regimes.
motivation: Gibbs state preparation is a fundamental computational technique in physics and statistics, and existing quantum samplers for commuting local Hamiltonians often rely on simulating the Davies generator, which may be inefficient in certain regimes.
method: The authors introduce a reduction from commuting quantum Hamiltonians to classical Hamiltonians, so that efficient classical Gibbs sampling suffices to efficiently prepare quantum Gibbs states, with explicit mappings for 2-local qudit CLHs and 4-local qubit CLHs on 2D lattices.
result: The sampler replicates state-of-the-art results and prepares Gibbs states in previously unknown regimes such as low temperature, exemplified by preparing the Gibbs state of the (defected) Toric code at any non-zero temperature in polynomial time.
conclusion: The reduction demonstrates that fast-mixing classical Gibbs samplers can enable efficient preparation of Gibbs states for many commuting quantum Hamiltonians, including highly entangled systems like the Toric code.

title: Streaming Belief Propagation On Mixed-Alphabet Tanner Graphs For Practical Quantum Memory
authors: Kao-Yueh Kuo And Ching-Yi Lai
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2207 (2026).

Reliable quantum memory under circuit-level noise requires decoders that can process syndrome information continuously and at a rate comparable to its generation. In practical quantum error correction (QEC), repeated syndrome measurements cause the number of potential error locations to grow rapidly with both code size and time. In this paper, we propose a streaming mixed-alphabet belief propagation (SM-BP) decoder. We construct a space-time Tanner graph across multiple rounds of syndrome extraction with mixed-alphabet error variables, preserving correlations arising from multi-qubit faults. Additionally, we propose an adaptive sliding window procedure that captures long error events across window boundaries and adjusts the decoding in real time. To enhance SM-BP, we introduce a technique of probabilistic error consolidation to mitigate degeneracy effects and short cycles. Our simulations demonstrate high error thresholds of 0.4% to 0.87% and strong error-floor performance for topological code families, including rotated toric, toric color, and twisted XZZX toric codes. These results show that SM-BP provides a practical decoding framework for continuous QEC under circuit-level noise.

.
tldr: The paper proposes a streaming mixed-alphabet belief propagation decoder for practical quantum memory under circuit-level noise.
motivation: Reliable quantum memory under circuit-level noise needs decoders that process syndrome information continuously and at a rate comparable to its generation, but repeated measurements make the number of potential error locations grow rapidly with code size and time.
method: It constructs a space-time Tanner graph with mixed-alphabet error variables to preserve multi-qubit fault correlations, uses an adaptive sliding window to capture long error events, and introduces probabilistic error consolidation to mitigate degeneracy and short cycles.
result: Simulations demonstrate high error thresholds of 0.4% to 0.87% and strong error-floor performance for rotated toric, toric color, and twisted XZZX toric codes.
conclusion: The streaming mixed-alphabet belief propagation decoder provides a practical framework for continuous quantum error correction under circuit-level noise.

title: Breaking The Orthogonality Barrier In Quantum Ldpc Codes
authors: Kenta Kasai
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2205 (2026).

Classical low-density parity-check (LDPC) codes are a widely deployed and well-established technology, forming the backbone of modern communication and storage systems. It is well known that, in this classical setting, increasing the girth of the Tanner graph while maintaining regular degree distributions leads simultaneously to good belief-propagation (BP) decoding performance and large minimum distance. In the quantum setting, however, this principle does not directly apply because quantum LDPC codes must satisfy additional orthogonality constraints between their parity-check matrices. When one enforces both orthogonality and regularity in a straightforward manner, the girth is typically reduced and the minimum distance becomes structurally upper bounded. In this work, we overcome this limitation by using permutation matrices with controlled commutativity and by restricting the orthogonality constraints to only the active part of the construction, while preserving regular check-matrix structures. This design circumvents conventional structural distance limitations induced by parent-matrix orthogonality, and enables the construction of quantum LDPC codes with large girth while avoiding latent low-weight logical operators. As a concrete demonstration, we construct a girth-8, (3,12)-regular [MATH] quantum LDPC code and show that, under BP decoding combined with a low-complexity post-processing algorithm, it achieves a frame error rate as low as [MATH] on the depolarizing channel with error probability [MATH].

.
tldr: A new construction of quantum LDPC codes overcomes the orthogonality barrier to achieve large girth and improved belief-propagation decoding performance.
motivation: Classical LDPC codes benefit from large girth, but quantum LDPC codes must satisfy orthogonality constraints that typically reduce girth and structurally limit minimum distance, hindering practical performance.
method: The paper uses permutation matrices with controlled commutativity and restricts orthogonality constraints to only the active part of the construction, preserving regular check-matrix structures and enabling large girth.
result: A girth-8, (3,12)-regular quantum LDPC code is constructed, and under BP decoding with low-complexity post-processing it achieves a frame error rate as low as 10^-5 on the depolarizing channel with error probability 0.1.
conclusion: The work demonstrates that high-girth quantum LDPC codes with good decoding performance are possible, advancing practical quantum error correction.

title: Heuristic And Optimal Synthesis Of Cnot And Clifford Circuits
authors: Mark Webster, Stergios Koutsioumpas, And Dan E Browne
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2212 (2026).

Efficiently implementing Clifford circuits is crucial for quantum error correction and quantum algorithms. Linear reversible circuits, equivalent to circuits composed of CNOT\xspace gates, have important applications in classical computing. In this work we present methods for CNOT\xspace and general Clifford circuit synthesis which can be used to minimise either the entangling two-qubit gate count or the circuit depth. We present three families of algorithms - optimal synthesis which works on small circuits, A* synthesis for intermediate-size circuits and greedy synthesis for large circuits. We benchmark against existing methods, including rustiq, tket and qiskit and show that our approach results in circuits with lower two-qubit gate count. For encoding circuits, our methods outperform previous reinforcement learning results and find a lower two-qubit gate count circuit for the Golay code than previously known. The algorithms have been implemented in a GitHub repository for use by the classical and quantum computing community.

GitHub Repository

.
tldr: The paper presents optimal, A*, and greedy algorithms for CNOT and Clifford circuit synthesis that minimize two-qubit gate count or depth, improving on existing tools for encoding circuits such as the Golay code.
motivation: Efficiently implementing Clifford circuits is crucial for quantum error correction and quantum algorithms, and minimizing entangling gates or depth reduces resource overhead.
method: Three families of synthesis algorithms are developed: optimal synthesis for small circuits, A* synthesis for intermediate sizes, and greedy synthesis for large circuits; they are benchmarked against rustiq, tket, and qiskit.
result: The methods produce circuits with lower two-qubit gate counts than existing approaches, outperform previous reinforcement learning results for encoding circuits, and find a lower two-qubit gate count circuit for the Golay code.
conclusion: The algorithms are implemented in a public GitHub repository, providing practical tools for the classical and quantum computing community to improve Clifford and CNOT circuit synthesis.

title: Simple Logical Quantum Computation With Concatenated Symplectic Double Codes
authors: Noah Berthusen And Elijah Durso-Sabina
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2195 (2026).

There have been significant recent advances in constructing theoretical and practical quantum error correcting codes that function well as quantum memories; however, performing fault-tolerant logical gates on these codes is less studied, and the protocols that do exist often require significant complexity. Building off the symplectic double construction, we investigate concatenated symplectic double codes, which have a rich set of logical gates implementable using only physical single-qubit gates and qubit relabeling. Combined with injected fold-transversal gates, the full Clifford group on a single codeblock is achieved through a functionally simple circuit. We perform circuit-level simulations of state preparation and quantum error correction on these codes and show that they have promising performance at near state-of-the-art physical error rates. As such, we argue that concatenated symplectic double codes are strong contenders as the underlying computational code on medium- to large-scale quantum computers.

.
tldr: The paper studies concatenated symplectic double codes, showing that a full Clifford group on a single codeblock can be achieved with simple physical single-qubit gates plus qubit relabeling and injected fold-transversal gates, with promising circuit-level performance.
motivation: Quantum error correcting codes that work well as memories are now well developed, but fault-tolerant logical gate implementations on them remain complex and less studied, motivating the search for codes with simple, low-overhead logical gate sets.
method: Building on the symplectic double construction, the authors analyze concatenated versions of these codes and design logical gate protocols using only physical single-qubit operations, qubit relabeling, and injected fold-transversal gates, then perform circuit-level simulations of state preparation and error correction.
result: The full Clifford group on a single codeblock is realized through a functionally simple circuit, and circuit-level simulations show competitive performance at near state-of-the-art physical error rates.
conclusion: Concatenated symplectic double codes are argued to be strong candidates as the underlying computational code for medium- to large-scale quantum computers.

title: Efficient Graph State Generation In Linear Optics
authors: Seungbeom Chin And William John Munro
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2189 (2026).

Graph states are central resources for quantum information processing, supporting applications in computation, communication, and error correction. In photonic systems, they are typically assembled from smaller entangled states using probabilistic fusion gates, which demand many photons and suffer from low success rates. We present an optimized scheme for directly generating caterpillar graph states (CGSs)—essential resource states for constructing high-dimensional lattice graph states—using only single-photon sources, linear optics, and heralded measurements. Based on the linear quantum graph (LQG) picture, our method produces CGSs efficiently. For CGSs of length [MATH], it requires [MATH] fewer photons and achieves a success rate [MATH] times higher than fusion-based approaches. These results demonstrate that the LQG picture provides a powerful and flexible route to generating complex photonic graph states for efficient quantum information processing.

.
tldr: The paper proposes an optimized linear-optics scheme to directly generate caterpillar graph states using single-photon sources and heralded measurements, outperforming fusion-based methods.
motivation: Graph states are key resources for quantum computation, communication, and error correction, but photonic generation via probabilistic fusion gates is photon-intensive and inefficient.
method: Using the linear quantum graph (LQG) picture, the authors design a direct generation protocol for caterpillar graph states with only single-photon sources, linear optics, and heralded measurements.
result: For length-M caterpillar graph states, the scheme requires fewer photons and achieves a success rate orders of magnitude higher than fusion-based approaches.
conclusion: The LQG approach offers a powerful and flexible route to generating complex photonic graph states for efficient quantum information processing.

title: Faster Quantum Simulation Of Markovian Open Quantum Systems Via Randomisation
authors: I.J. David, I. Sinayskiy, And F. Petruccione
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2204 (2026).

When simulating the dynamics of open quantum systems with quantum computers, it is essential to accurately approximate the system's behaviour while preserving the physicality of its evolution. Traditionally, for Markovian open quantum systems, this has been achieved using first and second-order Trotter-Suzuki product formulas or probabilistic algorithms. In this work, we introduce novel non-probabilistic algorithms for simulating Markovian open quantum systems using randomisation. Our methods, including first and second-order randomised Trotter-Suzuki formulas and the QDRIFT channel, not only maintain the physicality of the system's evolution but also enhance the scalability and precision of quantum simulations. We derive error bounds and step count limits for these techniques, bypassing the need for the mixing lemma typically employed in Hamiltonian simulation proofs. Furthermore, we implement these randomised algorithms using Classical Sampling (CS), demonstrating their gate complexity advantages over deterministic TS product formulas. This work systematically extends powerful randomisation techniques from Hamiltonian simulation to the general setting of Markovian open quantum systems, highlighting their potential to enable faster and more accurate simulations.

.
tldr: Introduces non-probabilistic randomised algorithms (first/second-order randomised Trotter-Suzuki and QDRIFT channel) for simulating Markovian open quantum systems, with error bounds and gate complexity advantages over deterministic Trotter-Suzuki.
motivation: Efficient quantum simulation of open quantum systems is challenging; existing methods using deterministic Trotter-Suzuki or probabilistic algorithms may be less scalable or precise.
method: Extends randomisation techniques from Hamiltonian simulation to Markovian open quantum systems, deriving error bounds and step count limits without the mixing lemma, and implements via Classical Sampling.
result: The randomised algorithms maintain physicality of evolution, achieve better gate complexity than deterministic product formulas, and provide rigorous error bounds.
conclusion: Randomisation offers a faster and more accurate route for simulating Markovian open quantum dynamics on quantum computers.

title: Catalytic $z$-rotations In Constant $T$-depth
authors: Isaac H. Kim
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2191 (2026).

We show that the [MATH]-depth of any single-qubit [MATH]-rotation can be reduced to [MATH] if a certain catalyst state is available. To achieve an [MATH]-approximation, it suffices to have a catalyst state of size polynomial in [MATH]. This implies that [MATH] admits a finite universal gate set consisting of Clifford+[MATH]. In particular, there are catalytic constant [MATH]-depth circuits that approximate multi-qubit Toffoli, adder, and quantum Fourier transform arbitrarily well. We also show that the catalyst state can be prepared in time polynomial in [MATH].

.
tldr: Catalytic states can reduce the T-depth of arbitrary single-qubit z-rotations to constant, enabling efficient Clifford+T approximations of important quantum circuits.
motivation: Reducing T-depth is crucial for fault-tolerant quantum computing, but many rotations require deep T-gate sequences. Catalysts offer a way to achieve constant depth without consuming the catalyst.
method: The paper constructs a catalyst state of polynomial size (in 1/epsilon) that enables constant T-depth approximation of any single-qubit z-rotation, and shows the catalyst can be prepared in polynomial time.
result: Constant T-depth is achievable for z-rotations, implying a finite universal gate set of Clifford+T and enabling catalytic constant T-depth circuits for multi-qubit Toffoli, adder, and quantum Fourier transform.
conclusion: Catalytic z-rotations provide a powerful tool for constant-depth quantum circuits, with potential applications in fault-tolerant quantum computing architectures.

title: Quantum Resource Comparison For Two Leading Surface Code Lattice Surgery Approaches
authors: Tyler Leblond And Ryan S. Bennink
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2187 (2026).

Hamiltonian simulation is one of the most promising candidates for the demonstration of quantum advantage within the next ten years, and several studies have proposed end-to-end resource estimates for executing such algorithms on fault-tolerant quantum processors. Usually, these resource estimates are based upon the assumption that quantum error correction is implemented using the surface code, and that the best surface code compilation scheme involves serializing input circuits by eliminating all Clifford gates. This transformation is thought to make best use of the native multi-body measurement (lattice surgery) instruction set available to surface codes. Some work, however, has suggested that direct compilation from Clifford+T to lattice surgery operations may be beneficial for circuits that have high degrees of logical parallelism. In this study, we analyze the resource costs for implementing Hamiltonian simulation using example approaches from each of these leading surface code compilation families. The Hamiltonians whose dynamics we consider are those of the transverse-field Ising model in several geometries, the Kitaev honeycomb model, and the [MATH] complex under a time-varying magnetic field. We show, among other things, that the optimal scheme depends on whether Hamiltonian simulation is implemented using the quantum signal processing or Trotter-Suzuki algorithms, with Trotterization benefiting by orders of magnitude from direct Clifford+T compilation for these applications. Our results suggest that surface code quantum computers should not have a one-size-fits-all compilation scheme, but that smart compilers should predict the optimal scheme based upon high-level quantities from logical circuits such as average circuit density, numbers of logical qubits, and T fraction.

.
tldr: This paper compares resource costs of two leading surface code lattice surgery compilation approaches for Hamiltonian simulation, finding that the optimal scheme depends on the simulation algorithm and circuit characteristics.
motivation: Fault-tolerant quantum computing resource estimates often assume serialized Clifford+T circuits for surface code lattice surgery, but direct Clifford+T compilation may benefit highly parallel circuits. The authors aim to determine which compilation family is more efficient for Hamiltonian simulation applications.
method: The authors analyze resource costs for Hamiltonian simulation of transverse-field Ising models, the Kitaev honeycomb model, and a complex Hamiltonian under time-varying magnetic fields, comparing serialized Clifford gates versus direct Clifford+T to lattice surgery operations, and considering quantum signal processing versus Trotter-Suzuki algorithms.
result: They show that the optimal scheme depends on the simulation algorithm: Trotterization benefits by orders of magnitude from direct Clifford+T compilation for these applications, while quantum signal processing may favor serialization.
conclusion: Surface code quantum computers should not use a one-size-fits-all compilation scheme; smart compilers should predict the optimal scheme based on logical circuit metrics such as average circuit density, number of logical qubits, and T fraction.

title: Generalising Aumann’s Agreement Theorem
authors: Matthew Leifer And Cristhiano Duarte
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2210 (2026).

According to Aumann's celebrated theorem, rational agents cannot agree to disagree. In other words, agents who once shared a common prior probability distribution and who have common knowledge about their posteriors cannot assign different probability distributions to a given proposition. Common knowledge imposes strong restrictions on assigned probabilities. In fact, Aumann's agreement theorem was one of the first attempts to formalise and explore the role played by common knowledge in decision theory. Recently, the debate over possible (quantum) extensions of Aumann's results has resurfaced. This paper contributes to this discussion. First, we argue that agreeing to disagree is impossible in quantum theory. Secondly, by building on the quantum argument, we show that agreeing to disagree is also forbidden in any generalised probability theory. The upshot is that in its probabilistic version, the agreement theorem is a direct consequence of how we choose to condition upon acquiring new information.

.
tldr: The paper proves that rational agents cannot agree to disagree in quantum theory and in any generalised probabilistic theory, extending Aumann's agreement theorem.
motivation: Aumann's agreement theorem formalises how common knowledge restricts rational beliefs; recent debate about possible quantum extensions motivates a general probabilistic investigation.
method: The authors analyse common knowledge and posterior distributions within quantum theory and generalised probabilistic frameworks, arguing that the impossibility of agreeing to disagree follows from the conditioning rule.
result: They show that agreeing to disagree is impossible in quantum theory and, building on that argument, in any generalised probability theory.
conclusion: The probabilistic version of Aumann's agreement theorem is not specifically quantum but is a direct consequence of how agents condition upon acquiring new information.

title: Measurement Incompatibility In Bayesian Multiparameter Quantum Estimation
authors: Francesco Albarelli, Dominic Branford, And Jesús Rubio
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2192 (2026).

We present a comprehensive and pedagogical formulation of Bayesian multiparameter quantum estimation. Within this framework, we analyse the role of measurement incompatibility and establish its quantitative effect on attainable precision. We achieve this by deriving upper bounds based on the pretty good measurement – a notion from hypothesis testing – combined with the evaluation of the Nagaoka-Hayashi lower bound. In general, we prove that, as in the many-copy regime of local estimation theory, incompatibility can at most double the minimum loss relative to the idealised scenario in which individually optimal measurements are assumed jointly implementable. Therefore, in practical situations, the latter may provide a sufficient and computationally efficient benchmark without solving the full optimisation problem. Our results, which we illustrate through applications of discrete phase imaging, phase and dephasing estimation, and qubit sensing, provide analytical and numerical tools for assessing ultimate precision limits and the role of measurement incompatibility in Bayesian multiparameter quantum metrology, including an open-source package for all the bounds discussed here.

.
tldr: The paper develops a Bayesian framework for multiparameter quantum estimation and quantifies how measurement incompatibility limits attainable precision.
motivation: Multiparameter quantum estimation is fundamental to quantum metrology, but incompatible optimal measurements can prevent achieving ideal precision, so quantifying this limitation is important.
method: The authors derive upper bounds using the pretty good measurement from hypothesis testing and evaluate the Nagaoka-Hayashi lower bound, comparing joint measurements with individually optimal ones.
result: They prove that measurement incompatibility can at most double the minimum loss relative to the ideal joint-measurement scenario, and illustrate the results with discrete phase imaging, phase and dephasing estimation, and qubit sensing.
conclusion: The work provides analytical and numerical tools, including an open-source package, for assessing ultimate precision limits and the role of measurement incompatibility in Bayesian multiparameter quantum metrology.

title: Robust Topological Quantum State Transfer With Long-range Interactions In Rydberg Arrays
authors: Siri Raupach, Beatriz Olmos, And Mathias B. M. Svendsen
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2190 (2026).

We develop a theoretical framework for fast, robust and high-fidelity topological quantum state transfer in one-dimensional systems with long-range couplings, motivated by chains of Rydberg atoms with dipole–dipole interactions. Such long-range interactions naturally give rise to extended Su–Schrieffer–Heeger and Rice–Mele models supporting topologically protected edge states. We show that these edge states enable high-fidelity edge-to-edge excitation transfer using both time-independent protocols, based on coherent edge state dynamics, and time-dependent protocols, based on adiabatic modulation of system parameters. Long-range couplings play a central role by enhancing the relevant energy gaps, leading to a substantial improvement in transfer efficiency compared to nearest neighbour models. The resulting transfer is robust against positional disorder, reflecting its topological origin and highlighting the potential of long-range interacting platforms for reliable quantum state transfer.

.
tldr: Develops topological quantum state transfer protocols in long-range Rydberg arrays using extended SSH and Rice-Mele edge states.
motivation: Reliable quantum state transfer is essential for quantum information processing, and Rydberg arrays with long-range dipole-dipole interactions offer a promising platform with topological protection.
method: Theoretically analyzes one-dimensional extended SSH and Rice-Mele models with long-range couplings, using both time-independent coherent edge-state dynamics and time-dependent adiabatic parameter modulation.
result: Long-range couplings enhance the relevant energy gaps and substantially improve transfer efficiency compared to nearest-neighbour models, while the transfer remains robust against positional disorder.
conclusion: Long-range interacting Rydberg arrays are promising for robust, high-fidelity topological quantum state transfer, highlighting their potential for reliable quantum information tasks.

title: Reducing Spatial And Temporal Dimensionality In The Multidimensional Caldeira-Leggett Model
authors: Hongfei Zhan, Ernest W.Z. Pan, And Zhenning Cai
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2201 (2026).

Focusing on the real-time dynamics of the reduced density matrix of the multidimensional Caldeira-Leggett model, several techniques are adopted in this paper to reduce the spatial and temporal dimensionality, combined into an efficient algorithm. From a spatial perspective, an equivalent formulation of the Dyson series is presented. With the aid of a low-rank approximation, the spatial dimensionality of open quantum system simulations is halved. From a temporal perspective, the frozen Gaussian approximation is used to approximate both the evolution operator and the interaction operator in the multidimensional Caldeira-Leggett model. This reduces the high-dimensional integrals to one- and two-dimensional integrals independent of the truncation level of the Dyson series. Through these techniques, we design an efficient algorithm whose validity is verified through several numerical experiments, including a two-dimensional double slit simulation.

.
tldr: This paper develops an efficient algorithm for simulating the real-time dynamics of the reduced density matrix in the multidimensional Caldeira-Leggett model by reducing spatial and temporal dimensionality.
motivation: Simulating open quantum systems in multiple dimensions is computationally challenging due to the high dimensionality of the reduced density matrix and the memory effects in the Caldeira-Leggett model.
method: The authors introduce an equivalent Dyson series formulation combined with low-rank approximation to halve the spatial dimensionality, and use the frozen Gaussian approximation to reduce high-dimensional integrals to one- and two-dimensional integrals independent of the Dyson truncation level.
result: Numerical experiments, including a two-dimensional double-slit simulation, verify the validity and efficiency of the proposed algorithm.
conclusion: The method provides a practical and efficient computational tool for studying real-time dynamics in multidimensional open quantum systems, with potential applications in quantum thermodynamics and decoherence studies.

title: Unconditional Quantum Advantage For Sampling With Shallow Circuits
authors: Adam Bene Watts And Natalie Parham
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2188 (2026).

Recent work by Bravyi, Gosset, and Koenig showed that there exists a search problem that a constant-depth quantum circuit can solve, but that any constant-depth classical circuit with bounded fan-in cannot. They also pose the question: Can we achieve a similar proof of separation for an input-independent sampling task? In this paper, we show that the answer to this question is yes when the number of random input bits given to the classical circuit is bounded. We introduce a distribution [MATH] over [MATH] and construct a constant-depth uniform quantum circuit family [MATH] such that [MATH] samples from a distribution close to [MATH] in total variation distance. For any [MATH] we also prove, unconditionally, that any classical circuit with bounded fan-in gates that takes as input [MATH] i.i.d. Bernouli random variables with entropy [MATH] and produces output close to [MATH] in total variation distance has depth [MATH]. This gives an unconditional proof that constant-depth quantum circuits can sample from distributions that can't be reproduced by constant-depth bounded fan-in classical circuits, even up to additive error. We also show a similar separation between constant-depth quantum circuits with advice and classical circuits with bounded fan-in and fan-out, but access to an unbounded number of i.i.d random inputs. The distribution [MATH] and classical circuit lower bounds are inspired by work of Viola, in which he shows a different (but related) distribution cannot be sampled from approximately by constant-depth bounded fan-in classical circuits.

.
tldr: The paper proves an unconditional separation between constant-depth quantum circuits and bounded fan-in classical circuits for an input-independent sampling task.
motivation: Bravyi, Gosset, and Koenig showed a search problem solvable by constant-depth quantum but not classical circuits, and asked whether a similar separation exists for sampling tasks.
method: The authors construct a distribution over {0,1}^n and a constant-depth uniform quantum circuit family that samples from it, then prove unconditional depth lower bounds for bounded fan-in classical circuits, inspired by Viola's work.
result: Constant-depth quantum circuits can sample from distributions that cannot be approximated by constant-depth bounded fan-in classical circuits even up to additive error, and a similar separation holds with advice and unbounded random inputs.
conclusion: This provides an unconditional quantum advantage for shallow-circuit sampling, answering the open question and extending circuit separations to sampling tasks.

title: Sparse Quantum State Preparation With Improved Toffoli Cost
authors: Felix Rupprecht And Sabine Wölk
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2208 (2026).

The preparation of quantum states is one of the most fundamental tasks in quantum computing, and a key primitive in many quantum algorithms. Of particular interest to areas such as quantum simulation and linear-system solvers are sparse quantum states, which contain only a small number [MATH] of non-zero computational basis states compared to a generic state. In this work, we present an approach that prepares [MATH]-sparse states on [MATH] qubits, reducing the number of Toffoli gates required compared to prior art. We work in the established framework of first preparing a dense state on a [MATH]-qubit sub-register, and then mapping this state to the target state via an isometry, with the latter step dominating the cost of the full algorithm. The speed-up is achieved by designing an efficient algorithm for finding and implementing the isometry. The worst-case Toffoli cost of our isometry circuit, which may be viewed as a batched version of an approach by Malvetti et al., is essentially [MATH] for sufficiently large values of [MATH], yielding roughly a [MATH] improvement factor over the state-of-the-art. In numerical benchmarks on randomly chosen states, the cost is closer to [MATH]. With the improved isometry circuit, we examine the dense-state preparation step and present ways to optimize the joint cost of both steps, particularly in the case of target states with purely real coefficients, by outsourcing some sub-tasks from the dense-state preparation to the isometry.

.
tldr: The paper proposes an efficient method to prepare sparse quantum states on n qubits with reduced Toffoli gate cost by optimizing the isometry mapping from a dense sub-register state.
motivation: Sparse state preparation is a key primitive for quantum simulation and linear-system solvers, so reducing the Toffoli count is important for practical quantum algorithms.
method: The authors use a framework that first prepares a dense state on a log k-qubit sub-register and then applies an isometry to map it to the target k-sparse state, designing an improved algorithm for finding and implementing the isometry in a batched manner inspired by Malvetti et al.
result: Worst-case Toffoli cost is essentially improved over prior art by roughly a polynomial factor for sufficiently large parameters, with numerical benchmarks on random states showing even better practical scaling.
conclusion: The improved isometry circuit allows joint optimization of dense-state preparation and isometry steps, especially for target states with real coefficients, advancing efficient quantum state preparation.

title: Non-Gaussian Noise Magnetometry Using Local Spin Qubits
authors: Jonathan B. Curtis, Amir Yacoby, And Eugene Demler
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2197 (2026).

Atomic scale qubits, as may be realized in nitrogen vacancy (NV) centers in diamond, offer the opportunity to study magnetic field noise with nanometer scale spatial resolution. Using these spin qubits, one can learn a great deal about the magnetic-field noise correlations, and correspondingly the collective-mode spectra, in quantum materials and devices. However, to date these tools have been essentially restricted to studying Gaussian noise processes – equivalent to linear-response. In this work we will show how to extend these techniques beyond the Gaussian regime and show how to unambiguously measure higher-order magnetic noise cumulants in a local, spatially resolved way. We unveil two protocols for doing this; the first uses a single spin-qubit and different dynamical decoupling sequences to extract non-Markovian and non-Gaussian spin-echo noise. The second protocol uses two-qubit coincidence measurements to study spatially non-local cumulants in the magnetic noise. We then demonstrate the utility of these protocols by considering a model of a bath of non-interacting two-level systems, as well as a model involving spatially correlated magnetic fluctuations near a second-order Ising phase transition. In both cases, we highlight how this technique can be used to measure in a real many-body system how fluctuation dynamics converge towards the central limit theorem as a function of effective bath size. We then conclude by discussing some promising applications and extensions of this method.

.
tldr: The paper proposes protocols using single and two NV spin qubits to measure higher-order, non-Gaussian magnetic noise cumulants with nanoscale spatial resolution.
motivation: NV centers enable nanoscale magnetic field noise spectroscopy, but existing techniques are limited to Gaussian noise (linear response), restricting their applicability to non-linear and non-Gaussian regimes.
method: The authors use dynamical decoupling sequences with a single spin qubit to extract temporal non-Gaussian cumulants, and two-qubit coincidence measurements for spatially non-local cumulants, applied to models of non-interacting two-level systems and Ising critical fluctuations.
result: The protocols can unambiguously measure higher-order noise cumulants and reveal how fluctuation dynamics converge to the central limit theorem as the effective bath size increases.
conclusion: This work extends quantum magnetometry beyond linear response and provides new tools to probe non-Gaussian and spatially correlated fluctuations in quantum materials.

title: Quantum Max d-Cut Via Qudit Swap Operators
authors: Igor Klep, Tea Štrekelj, And Jurij Volčič
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2203 (2026).

Quantum Max Cut (QMC) problem for systems of qubits is an example of a 2-local Hamiltonian problem, and a prominent paradigm in computational complexity theory. This paper investigates the algebraic structure of a higher-dimensional analog of the QMC problem for systems of qudits. The Quantum Max [MATH]-Cut ([MATH]-QMC) problem asks for the largest eigenvalue of a Hamiltonian on a graph with [MATH] vertices whose edges correspond to swap operators acting on [MATH]. The algebra generated by the swap operators is identified as a quotient of a free algebra modulo symmetric group relations and a single additional relation of degree [MATH]. This presentation leads to a tailored hierarchy of semidefinite programs, leveraging noncommutative polynomial optimization (NPO) methods, that converges to the solution of the [MATH]-QMC problem. For a large class of complete bipartite graphs, exact solutions for the [MATH]-QMC problem are derived using the representation theory of symmetric groups and Littlewood-Richardson coefficients. Lastly, the paper addresses a refined [MATH]-QMC problem focused on finding the largest eigenvalue within each isotypic component (irreducible block) of the graph Hamiltonian. It is shown that the spectrum of the star graph Hamiltonian distinguishes between isotypic components of the [MATH]-QMC problem. For general [MATH], low-degree relations for separating isotypic components are presented, enabling adaptation of the global NPO hierarchy to efficiently compute the largest eigenvalue in each isotypic component.

.
tldr: The paper studies the algebraic structure and optimization hierarchy for Quantum Max d-Cut, a qudit generalization of Quantum Max Cut, using swap operators and symmetric group representation theory.
motivation: Quantum Max Cut is a prominent 2-local Hamiltonian problem in computational complexity theory, and extending it to qudits may reveal algebraic structure and enable efficient semidefinite programming hierarchies.
method: The authors characterize the algebra generated by swap operators as a quotient of a free algebra, build a noncommutative polynomial optimization (NPO) hierarchy of semidefinite programs, and use representation theory of symmetric groups and Littlewood-Richardson coefficients to solve complete bipartite graphs.
result: They derive exact solutions for a large class of complete bipartite graphs, show that the spectrum of the star graph Hamiltonian distinguishes isotypic components, and present low-degree relations to separate isotypic components for general dimension.
conclusion: The work provides algebraic and computational tools for the Quantum Max d-Cut problem, extending quantum Max Cut to qudits and enabling efficient computation within isotypic components.

title: A Brief History Of Quantum Vs Classical Computational Advantage
authors: Ryan Larose
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2198 (2026).

In this review article we summarize all experiments claiming quantum computational advantage to date. Our review highlights challenges, loopholes, and refutations appearing in subsequent work to provide a complete picture of the current statuses of these experiments. In addition, we also discuss theoretical computational advantage in example problems such as approximate optimization and recommendation systems. Finally, we review recent experiments in quantum error correction --- the biggest frontier to reach experimental quantum advantage in Shor's algorithm.

.
tldr: A review summarizing all experiments claiming quantum computational advantage to date, including challenges, loopholes, refutations, theoretical advantage examples, and recent quantum error correction experiments.
motivation: To provide a complete picture of the current statuses of quantum advantage experiments and to identify the remaining frontiers, especially quantum error correction for Shor's algorithm.
method: Survey and critical analysis of experimental claims of quantum computational advantage, theoretical computational advantage in approximate optimization and recommendation systems, and recent quantum error correction experiments.
result: Highlights loopholes and refutations in advantage claims, discusses theoretical speedups in example problems, and reviews quantum error correction as the biggest frontier for experimental quantum advantage.
conclusion: Quantum advantage claims require careful scrutiny, and achieving full advantage in Shor's algorithm depends on further advances in quantum error correction.

title: A Scheme For Deterministic Photon-photon Interaction Via Microresonator Phase Matching In AlGaAs-on-insulator Circuit
authors: Minghao Shang, Hua-Ying Liu, Shi-Ning Zhu And Zhenda Xie
abstract: Efficient photon-photon interaction towards 100% efficiency is a longstanding goal in optical quantum information processing, but remains challenging because of weak nonlinearity on current nonlinear optical platforms, or demanding requirements of on-chip microresonators. Here, we propose a scheme for deterministic photon-photon interaction (DPPI) by achieving microresonator phase matching, in an AlGaAs-on-insulator (AlGaAsOI) microdisk resonator. A 2.8 μm radius microdisk with a full air-cladding structure is used, for minimizing mode volume with low simulated bending loss. Strong structural dispersion engineering can be introduced in such small size, to achieve phase matching between TE and TM fundamental modes for maximal mode overlap. DPPI is therefore predicted with Q of only on the order of 4 × 106, providing a target for future fabrication development on the AlGaAsOI platform. Such scheme accesses the ultra-high material χ(2) coefficient of the III–V material integrated photonic platform, bringing in potential for full-integrated multi-function optical quantum chip towards many quantum information processing tasks.
tldr: A scheme for deterministic photon-photon interaction via microresonator phase matching in an AlGaAs-on-insulator microdisk is proposed for optical quantum information processing.
motivation: Efficient photon-photon interaction is a longstanding goal in optical quantum information processing, but weak nonlinearity on current platforms or demanding microresonator requirements hinder progress.
method: The authors use a 2.8 μm radius AlGaAs-on-insulator microdisk with full air-cladding and structural dispersion engineering to phase-match TE and TM fundamental modes for maximal mode overlap.
result: Deterministic photon-photon interaction is predicted with a quality factor of only ~4×10^6, providing a fabrication target for future AlGaAs-on-insulator development.
conclusion: The scheme exploits the ultra-high χ(2) of III–V materials for a fully integrated multifunction optical quantum chip, enabling various quantum information processing tasks.

title: Putting Machine Learning To The Test In A Quantum Many-body System
authors: Alberto Rodríguez And Rudolf A Römer Yilun Gao
abstract: Quantum many-body systems pose a formidable computational challenge due to the exponential growth of their Hilbert space. While deep learning (DL) has shown promise as an alternative paradigm, many applications in these systems are still to mature further, beyond the proof-of-concept stages of energy estimation at the lower end of the spectrum. Here, we extend DL beyond this frontier by extensively testing HubbardNet, a deep neural network architecture for the Bose–Hubbard model. Pushing improvements in the optimizer and learning rates, and introducing physics-informed output activations that can resolve extremely small wave-function amplitudes, we achieve ground-state energy errors reduced by orders of magnitude and wave-function fidelities exceeding 99%. We further assess physical relevance by analyzing generalized inverse participation ratios and multifractal dimensions for ground and excited states in one and two dimensions, demonstrating that optimized DL models reproduce localization, delocalization, and multifractality trends across the spectrum. Crucially, these qualitative predictions remain robust across four decades of the interaction strength, e.g. spanning across superfluid, Mott-insulating, as well as quantum chaotic regimes. Together, these results suggest DL as a viable qualitative predictor of many-body structure, complementing the quantitative strengths of exact diagonalization and tensor-network methods.
tldr: The paper extensively tests the HubbardNet deep learning architecture on the Bose-Hubbard model, achieving high-accuracy ground-state energies and wave-function fidelities while reproducing localization and multifractality trends.
motivation: Quantum many-body systems are computationally hard due to exponential Hilbert space growth, and deep learning offers a promising alternative that needs to move beyond proof-of-concept energy estimation.
method: The authors improve HubbardNet with better optimizers, learning rates, and physics-informed output activations that resolve small wave-function amplitudes, then compute ground and excited states and analyze generalized inverse participation ratios and multifractal dimensions in one and two dimensions.
result: They reduce ground-state energy errors by orders of magnitude, achieve wave-function fidelities above 99%, and reproduce localization, delocalization, and multifractality trends across four decades of interaction strength, spanning superfluid, Mott-insulating, and quantum chaotic regimes.
conclusion: Deep learning can serve as a viable qualitative predictor of many-body structure, complementing exact diagonalization and tensor-network methods.

title: Solving The Nonlinear Vlasov Equation On A Quantum Computer
authors: Tamás Vaszary, Animesh Datta, Tom Goffrey, And Brian Appelbe
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2206 (2026).

The practical applicability of a recent Carleman-linearization-based quantum algorithm for solving ordinary differential equations (ODEs) with quadratic nonlinearities is investigated for the nonlinear electrostatic Vlasov equation with Krook-type collision operators. The equation is discretized on a (1+1)-dimensional phase-space grid and mapped onto the input of the quantum algorithm. Upper bounds for the query and gate complexities are derived in the limit of large grid sizes and found to be polynomially larger than the time complexity of the corresponding classical algorithms, primarily due to the dimension, sparsity, and norm of the Carleman-linearized evolution matrix. The convergence criteria are shown to impose severe restrictions on physically relevant plasma applications, requiring dissipation levels far exceeding those provided by the Krook operator.

.
tldr: This paper investigates the practical applicability of a Carleman-linearization-based quantum algorithm for solving the nonlinear electrostatic Vlasov equation with Krook collisions, finding it polynomially slower than classical methods and impractical for realistic plasma parameters.
motivation: Quantum algorithms have been proposed for solving differential equations, but their practical utility for physically relevant nonlinear plasma problems remains unclear.
method: The nonlinear Vlasov equation is discretized on a (1+1)-dimensional phase-space grid and mapped onto a recent Carleman-linearization quantum algorithm for ODEs with quadratic nonlinearities; query and gate complexity bounds are derived for large grids.
result: The quantum algorithm's complexity is polynomially larger than that of classical algorithms due to the dimension, sparsity, and norm of the Carleman-linearized matrix, and convergence criteria demand dissipation levels far exceeding what Krook-type collisions provide.
conclusion: The studied quantum algorithm offers no practical advantage for solving the nonlinear Vlasov equation in physically relevant plasma regimes, highlighting significant limitations of current Carleman-linearization approaches.

title: Temporal Coupled-mode Theory And Topological Charges For Resonances In Parity Symmetric Layered Media With Arbitrary Loss And Gain
authors: Tiecheng Wang And Yichi Zhang
abstract: The traditional temporal coupled-mode theory (TCMT) is used to explain the resonances in the resonators where material loss or gain is zero or small, such that the energy of the resonance is exactly or approximately conserved. However, with the development of non-Hermitian optical theories and experiments, a more widely applicable TCMT is required. In this work, we derive the TCMT suitable for parity symmetric layered structures with arbitrary degrees of non-Hermiticity, and obtain specific expressions for the transmissions and reflections of the original and its time-reversed cavities. The simulated results calculated by the scattering matrix method agree well with our theoretical predictions, proving the validity of our theory. Moreover, we find that in the space spanned by frequency and decay rate, there are poles where transmission and reflection tend to infinity simultaneously and zeros where reflection is zero in real frequency, their positions and topological properties can all be clearly explained by our theory. We believe that our research provides an important theoretical foundation for the applications of non-Hermitian media such as Fabry–Pérot cavity with arbitrary loss and gain.
tldr: The paper develops a generalized temporal coupled-mode theory for parity-symmetric layered media with arbitrary loss and gain, explaining resonance poles, zeros, and their topological properties.
motivation: Traditional temporal coupled-mode theory assumes weak or zero loss/gain, so non-Hermitian optical systems with strong loss and gain require a more general framework.
method: The authors derive an extended temporal coupled-mode theory for parity-symmetric layered structures and compare it with scattering-matrix simulations.
result: The derived theory accurately predicts transmissions and reflections, and clarifies the positions and topological charges of poles and zeros in the frequency–decay-rate plane.
conclusion: This work provides a theoretical foundation for non-Hermitian optical devices such as Fabry–Pérot cavities with arbitrary loss and gain.

title: Truncation Uncertainties For Accurate Quantum Simulations Of Lattice Gauge Theories
authors: Anthony N. Ciavarella, Siddharth Hariprakash, Jad C. Halimeh, And Christian W. Bauer
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2216 (2026).

The encoding of lattice gauge theories onto quantum computers requires a discretization of the gauge field's Hilbert space on each link, which presents errors with respect to the Kogut–Susskind limit. In the electric basis, Hilbert space fragmentation has recently been shown to limit the excitation of large electric fields. Here, we leverage this to develop a formalism for estimating the size of truncation errors in the electric basis. Generically, the truncation error falls off as a factorial of the field truncation. Examples of this formalism are applied to the Schwinger model and a pure U(1) lattice gauge theory. For reasonable choices of parameters, we improve on previous error estimates by a factor of [MATH].

.
tldr: The paper develops a formalism for estimating truncation errors that arise when discretizing gauge fields on quantum computers for lattice gauge theory simulations.
motivation: Accurate quantum simulation of lattice gauge theories requires understanding and controlling errors from truncating the gauge field's Hilbert space relative to the Kogut–Susskind limit.
method: The authors leverage Hilbert space fragmentation in the electric basis to derive how truncation errors scale, applying the formalism to the Schwinger model and pure U(1) lattice gauge theory.
result: They find that truncation error falls off factorially with the field truncation and, for reasonable parameters, improve upon previous error estimates by a significant factor.
conclusion: This work provides practical tools for estimating truncation uncertainties in quantum simulations of lattice gauge theories, aiding in the design of accurate simulations.

title: Measuring A Quantum Measure Exceeding Unity
authors: Sanchari Chakraborti, Rafael D. Sorkin, And Urbasi Sinha
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2215 (2026).

The history based formalism known as Quantum Measure Theory (QMT) generalizes the concept of probability-measure so as to incorporate quantum interference. The resulting quantum measure [MATH] is defined for arbitrary events (sets of histories), not just for observables at a fixed moment of time.
